beats.narration_text: Making Water in Godot. Build a water shader one layer at a time, from flat blue to a see-through, foamy, wavy sea that knows where the shore is. By the end you can restyle it from the Inspector.

beats.narration_text: Six terms before we start. A shader is a small program the graphics card runs to decide how something is drawn. A vertex is a corner point of a shape. A pixel is one dot of the picture. A texture is an image a shader can read by address. U V is a point's address on the shape. And the renderer is the part of Godot that draws.

beats.narration_text: Each pixel is seventy percent water plus thirty percent of what is behind it. We checked one pixel, water over sand. The blend predicts one hundred eight, one twenty-nine, one sixty-one. The screen reads one hundred eight, one twenty-nine, one sixty-two.

Under them two number rows: 'predicted 108, 129, 161' and 'screen 108, 129, 162'. Right: the real Forward+ test render (captures/blend-fp.png through lab_window) with one grey-backed terracotta ring on the probe point (plate over sand). Every number is a measured or computed figure from FACTCHECK.

beats.narration_text: Transparency has a price. Godot draws see-through objects after solid ones, sorted by each node's position, not pixel by pixel. This red plane lies under the water, but its node is nearer, so it draws on top. Let the water write depth, and it vanishes instead.

beats.narration_text: The docs add two more costs. Transparent materials cast no shadows, and they never appear in the depth or screen textures other shaders read. The second one matters soon: the water will read depth to see what lies beneath it.

beats.narration_text: Foam needs noise, and Godot's shading language has none. No noise function, and no Voronoi node: we counted one hundred ten visual shader nodes in Godot four point seven point two, and none makes noise. So we write one.

beats.narration_text: Here is the plan. Cut the surface into squares and put one point in each, at a random spot. Foam will live along the lines where two points are equally close.

Labels: 'one point each'. Drawn, not rendered: labelled 'drawing'.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. Blue is albedo, and a uniform makes it a dial. Writing alpha makes water see-through, and the renderer decides how it blends. Foam is cellular noise: the gap between the nearest and second nearest point. A normal map lights the ripples, and it can push the foam's address too. Real waves move vertices, and a script runs the same function for floaters. The depth texture tells the water where it meets the shore.
